jsonData.question: Which of the following correctly identifies all four main sources of uncertainty in robotics?
options: Sensor noise, actuator noise, environmental changes, and model inaccuracy
Sensor noise, rapid battery drainage, CPU clock errors, and network jitter
Actuator noise, signal interference, incorrect map data, and power supply issues
Sensor noise, programming mistakes, environmental changes, and data corruption
jsonData.explanation: The lecture defines exactly four sources: (1) Sensor noise — imperfect measurements, (2) Actuator noise — imperfect motion execution, (3) Environmental changes — the world is dynamic, (4) Model inaccuracy — simplified physics. The distractors substitute irrelevant causes like CPU errors or battery drainage, which are not in this framework.

jsonData.question: In a Gaussian distribution used to model robot sensor readings, what does σ² (variance) represent?
options: The most likely sensor value — the robot's single best estimate of the true measurement
The level of uncertainty — how spread out the probability distribution is around the mean
The total number of individual readings averaged to construct the distribution
The maximum distance between the highest and lowest observed sensor readings
jsonData.explanation: σ² (variance) represents how unsure the robot is — the spread of the bell curve. μ (mean) is the robot's best guess. Students frequently confuse them: the mean locates the distribution's center while variance describes its width (uncertainty level).

jsonData.question: Why is the Gaussian distribution described as 'Robotics' Best Friend' in the context of sensor noise modeling?
options: Because it can simultaneously represent multiple hypotheses at several different spatial locations
Because it requires no parameters to define and applies universally to every type of distribution
Because real sensor errors mostly cluster near zero, with large errors becoming progressively rarer
Because it guarantees sensor readings remain within a known bounded error range at all times
jsonData.explanation: The key intuition from the lecture: 'Most of the time, sensors are mostly right, sometimes a little wrong, rarely very wrong.' This matches the bell curve — small errors near zero are common, large errors are rare. Option A describes multimodal distributions; a Gaussian has exactly one peak.

jsonData.question: If P(Wet Floor | Rain) = 0.9 and P(Rain) = 0.3, what is P(Wet Floor AND Rain)?
options: 0.9 — the same as the conditional probability P(Wet Floor | Rain) already given
0.6 — computed by subtracting P(Rain) from P(Wet Floor | Rain)
0.3 — the marginal probability of rain occurring alone, without knowing floor state
0.27 — computed as P(Wet Floor | Rain) × P(Rain) = 0.9 × 0.3
jsonData.explanation: Joint probability P(A AND B) = P(A|B) × P(B). Substituting: 0.9 × 0.3 = 0.27. Students frequently confuse the joint probability with the conditional probability (0.9), or attempt addition instead of multiplication.

jsonData.question: What is the fundamental reason deterministic robot programming fails in real-world deployments?
options: It assumes sensors are perfectly accurate and that motor commands execute without any error
It requires storing excessively large probability distributions in memory at every time step
It cannot handle environments with more than a fixed number of discrete possible states
It relies on Gaussian assumptions that do not hold for digital sensor hardware outputs
jsonData.explanation: Deterministic programming assumes the same input always produces the same output — no noise, no uncertainty. In reality, 'Sensors NEVER read exactly 1.5!' The condition 'if sensor_reading == 1.5' will never be satisfied by a real noisy sensor, causing the program to fail.

jsonData.question: Compared to parametric belief representation, non-parametric (particle) representation is better suited for situations where:
options: Memory is severely limited and the robot needs very fast real-time computation
The belief distribution has multiple peaks due to ambiguous sensor information
The robot's position is already known with high confidence and minimal uncertainty
The environment is perfectly static, well-mapped, and free of any dynamic obstacles
jsonData.explanation: Non-parametric (particle) representation can model any distribution shape, including multimodal distributions with multiple peaks. Parametric representation assumes a single-peaked Gaussian, which fails when the robot cannot distinguish between identical landmarks (e.g., identical doors in a corridor).

jsonData.question: In Bayes' Rule P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B), what role does P(B) play?
options: It represents the prior belief about hypothesis A before any observation is made
It measures how probable hypothesis A is after observing the evidence B
A normalization constant ensuring all posterior probabilities sum to exactly 1
It measures how well hypothesis A explains the observed sensor evidence B
jsonData.explanation: P(B) is the total probability of observing evidence B across all hypotheses. It acts as a normalization constant ensuring the posterior probabilities across all hypotheses sum to 1. Without it, the numerator P(B|A)P(A) is an unnormalized product. Students often confuse P(B) with the likelihood P(B|A).

jsonData.question: A robot in a corridor with four identical doors receives a sensor reading of 'door detected.' Which belief representation is most appropriate and why?
options: Parametric (μ, σ²), because it is computationally fast and memory-efficient for real-time use
Parametric (μ, σ²), because sensor Gaussian noise is the dominant uncertainty in this scenario
Non-parametric (particles), because the belief converges to one narrow peak at the most likely door location
Non-parametric (particles), because the robot has multimodal uncertainty and could be near any door
jsonData.explanation: Identical doors cause ambiguity — 'door detected' is consistent with being at any of the four doors. The resulting belief is multimodal (one peak per door). A single Gaussian (parametric) cannot represent this correctly; particle filters (non-parametric) handle any distribution shape including multiple peaks.

jsonData.question: What is the memory complexity of a probabilistic robot that applies the Markov Assumption?
options: O(1) — only the previous state and current control input need to be stored
O(t) — the full sequence of states and actions must be retained over time
O(n²) — where n is the total number of positions in the environment map
O(log t) — because the history is compressed into a binary tree structure
jsonData.explanation: With the Markov Assumption P(xt | xt-1, ut), the robot only needs the previous state and current control input — a constant amount regardless of operating time. Without the assumption, memory grows as O(t) with every time step, becoming impractical for long-running robots.

jsonData.question: The Markov Property in probabilistic robotics states that:
options: The robot's current state depends on the complete history of all past states and all previous control inputs
The future state is conditionally independent of the entire past history, given only the current state
All sensor measurements are statistically independent of each other in all operating conditions
The environment must remain stationary between any two consecutive robot sensor readings
jsonData.explanation: The Markov Property: 'The future is independent of the past, given the present.' Only the current state matters for predicting the next state — the full history adds no information. This reduces memory from O(t) to O(1) and enables efficient recursive Bayesian estimation.

jsonData.question: A robot at Shelf 5 has a narrow, confident probability distribution. After executing 'move forward 1 shelf,' what happens to its belief distribution?
options: The distribution narrows further and its peak shifts forward to exactly Shelf 6
The distribution maintains its current width but its peak shifts forward toward Shelf 6
The distribution widens (more uncertainty) and its peak shifts forward toward Shelf 6
The distribution splits into two equal peaks, one at Shelf 5 and one at Shelf 6
jsonData.explanation: During the prediction step, actuator noise is added: wheels may slip, motors may over/under-rotate, floor friction may vary. The result is increased variance (wider distribution) — the robot is less certain of its exact position after moving. The peak shifts forward but the distribution spreads out.

jsonData.question: Which statement correctly describes the effect of each step in the Bayes Filter cycle used in robot localization?
options: Prediction decreases positional uncertainty; Correction increases it from sensor noise
Both prediction and correction progressively decrease uncertainty over time
Prediction uses sensor data to narrow estimates; Correction shifts estimates using motion commands
Prediction increases uncertainty due to motion noise; Correction decreases it via sensor measurements
jsonData.explanation: The lecture table: Prediction (Motion) → Uncertainty increases. Measurement (Sensors) → Uncertainty decreases. These two steps balance each other. A very common exam error is reversing which step increases vs. decreases uncertainty — motion makes things less certain; sensing makes things more certain.

jsonData.question: A robot has prior beliefs P(Near) = 0.5 and P(Far) = 0.5. The sensor model gives P(z=2m | Near) = 0.8 and P(z=2m | Far) = 0.2. After observing z=2m, what is P(Near | z)?
options: 0.8 — computed as (0.8 × 0.5) / 0.5 using Bayes' Rule
0.4 — computed as 0.8 × 0.5, the unnormalized joint probability before dividing
0.5 — the prior is unchanged because both hypotheses started equally likely
0.2 — the probability assigned to the Far hypothesis after the Bayesian update
jsonData.explanation: First, P(z) = P(z|N)P(N) + P(z|F)P(F) = (0.8)(0.5) + (0.2)(0.5) = 0.5. Then P(Near|z) = (0.8 × 0.5) / 0.5 = 0.4/0.5 = 0.8. The sensor strongly favors 'Near,' so the posterior rises from 0.5 to 0.8. Option B is the unnormalized numerator; option C incorrectly ignores the update.

jsonData.question: In Bayes-based robot localization, what does the Prior Probability P(A) represent?
options: The updated estimate of robot position computed after the most recent sensor reading
The robot's belief about its position before any new sensor measurement arrives
The probability of observing a specific sensor measurement given the robot is at position A
The normalization constant computed from summing all possible hypotheses about robot position
jsonData.explanation: P(A) is the prior — the robot's initial belief before new evidence. In localization, it comes from the previous time step's posterior (or prediction step). The posterior P(A|B) replaces it after each sensor update. Students often confuse prior with posterior — prior is BEFORE sensing, posterior is AFTER.

jsonData.question: The value P(sensor detects wall | robot is near wall) = 0.95 in a sensor model is classified as the:
options: Prior probability of the robot being near the wall before receiving any sensor data
Posterior probability of being near the wall after the sensor has detected the wall
The likelihood P(B|A) — probability of the observation given the robot position hypothesis
Evidence normalization factor from the denominator of the Bayes' Rule formula
jsonData.explanation: P(B|A) = 0.95 is the Likelihood — 'How probable is this observation if hypothesis A (near wall) is true?' It answers the sensor model question. Students often confuse this with the posterior P(A|B), which is what Bayes' Rule computes FROM the likelihood. Likelihood goes into Bayes' Rule; posterior comes out.

jsonData.question: A robot with limited processing power must estimate its position in real-time in a well-mapped building where uncertainty is unimodal. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Particle filter with 10,000 particles to guarantee the highest possible localization accuracy
Particle filter with 100 particles as a lightweight compromise between accuracy and speed
Hybrid approach that alternates between parametric and non-parametric on each sensing step
Parametric representation storing only μ and σ², using ~16 bytes with very fast computation
jsonData.explanation: When uncertainty is unimodal (Gaussian assumption holds), parametric representation is ideal: ~16 bytes, very fast computation. Particle filters use ~160,000 bytes for 10,000 particles and are significantly slower — overkill when the distribution is Gaussian. The trade-off is: speed+memory vs. flexibility.

jsonData.question: According to the lecture data, what is the approximate actuator error when a robot commanded to move 1 meter operates on a wet floor?
options: ±15%, significantly higher than on carpet or smooth surfaces
±5%, which is the same error level experienced on carpeted surfaces
±1%, approximately the same as operating on a perfectly smooth floor
±0.1%, because water provides a more consistent friction coefficient than dry surfaces
jsonData.explanation: Wet floor: ±15% error. Carpet: ±5%. Perfect floor: ±1%. This data from the lecture illustrates actuator noise — the same motor command produces different motion depending on surface conditions. The wet floor causes maximum slippage, which is why probabilistic models are essential for real environments.

jsonData.question: In the Bayesian Learning Loop, what happens to the posterior probability once it is computed from sensor evidence?
options: It is discarded after use, and the loop resets to a uniform prior distribution
It immediately becomes the new prior for the next iteration of the sensing cycle
It is averaged with the original prior to produce a smoothed, stable long-term estimate
It replaces the likelihood function to speed up computation in subsequent time steps
jsonData.explanation: The Bayesian loop is explicitly recursive: establish prior → gather evidence → update via Bayes' Rule → the posterior immediately becomes the prior for the next cycle. The diagram caption in the lecture states: 'The New Belief immediately becomes the Prior Belief for the next sensor reading.' The loop never resets.

jsonData.question: A robot inside a hallway with four identical doors receives the sensor reading 'door detected.' Which probability distribution type best represents its position belief?
options: Uniform distribution, since all hallway positions become equally probable after sensing
Gaussian distribution with a single peak centered at the nearest door to the starting point
Multimodal distribution with a separate probability peak at each door location
A single narrow Gaussian peak that sharpens progressively at the most recently visited door
jsonData.explanation: Identical doors create sensor ambiguity — 'door detected' is equally consistent with being at any of the four doors. The resulting belief has multiple separate peaks (multimodal). A single Gaussian cannot represent this correctly. Particle filters (non-parametric) are needed for such multimodal beliefs.

jsonData.question: The simplified motion model 'position = velocity × time' is best classified as which source of uncertainty?
options: Sensor noise, because the position estimate relies on inaccurate distance measurements
Actuator noise, because wheel slippage and motor variation cause positional execution errors
Environmental change, because floor conditions alter the velocity-displacement relationship
Model inaccuracy, since the formula ignores friction, battery voltage drops, and tire wear
jsonData.explanation: Model inaccuracy means the mathematical model oversimplifies reality. The simple formula position = velocity × time ignores friction (varies with floor), battery voltage (drops over time), tire pressure, floor slipping (±1°), and air resistance. These factors make the model wrong even if sensors and actuators are perfect.

jsonData.question: A student argues: 'Upgrading to sensors with only ±0.1% error lets us safely use deterministic programming.' What is the fundamental flaw in this reasoning?
options: Actuator noise, environment changes, and model inaccuracy persist even when sensors are highly accurate
Improving sensors to ±0.1% accuracy would simultaneously eliminate actuator noise and environmental uncertainty
Deterministic programming actually becomes more complex as sensor accuracy increases beyond a threshold
The Markov Assumption requires imperfect sensors to maintain statistical independence between time steps
jsonData.explanation: Sensor noise is only one of four uncertainty sources. Even with perfect sensors, wheels still slip (actuator noise), environments still change dynamically, and simplified models still misrepresent physics. Eliminating sensor noise alone does not make the world deterministic — it only removes one of four problems.

jsonData.question: A robot's sensor model gives P(Door | vertical line detected) = 0.95. The robot detects a vertical line. Which statement correctly interprets this?
options: The robot is certain it found a door, since 0.95 exceeds the minimum 0.9 confidence threshold
The robot updates its belief: there is a 95% probability this vertical feature is a door
This reading should be discarded because a 5% error rate is too high for reliable navigation
The value 0.95 is the prior probability that any detected feature in this environment is a door
jsonData.explanation: P(Door | vertical line) = 0.95 is a conditional probability used to update belief via Bayes' Rule. It is NOT a certainty guarantee (0.95 ≠ 1.0), NOT a prior (it conditions on observed evidence), and 5% residual uncertainty is normal and handled naturally within probabilistic frameworks.

jsonData.question: Without the Markov Assumption, why is real-time robot state estimation impractical?
options: The robot must also store a complete probability distribution over all possible map positions
Bayes' Rule cannot be mathematically derived without conditional independence between observations
Memory grows as O(t), requiring storage of every past state and control input ever executed
The sensor model P(z|x) changes with each new time step, making prior sensor data invalid
jsonData.explanation: Without the Markov Assumption, the state update requires P(xt | x0, x1, ..., xt-1, u0, ..., ut) — the full history. As time t grows, so does the memory requirement: O(t). For a robot operating for hours at high frequency, this becomes completely impractical for real-time computation.

jsonData.question: Using the lecture example (P(N)=0.5, P(F)=0.5, P(z=2|N)=0.8, P(z=2|F)=0.2), what is the total evidence probability P(z=2)?
options: 0.8 — the likelihood of observing z=2m when the robot is near the wall
0.4 — the joint probability P(z=2 AND Near) from the Near hypothesis alone
0.1 — the joint probability P(z=2 AND Far) from the Far hypothesis alone
jsonData.explanation: Total probability: P(z) = P(z|N)P(N) + P(z|F)P(F) = (0.8)(0.5) + (0.2)(0.5) = 0.4 + 0.1 = 0.5. This denominator normalizes both posterior probabilities. Options A, B, and C are component values (likelihood, Near joint prob, Far joint prob) — not the combined evidence term.

jsonData.question: Why does parametric belief representation require only ~16 bytes while particle-based representation requires ~160,000 bytes?
options: Parametric stores only two numbers (μ and σ²), while each particle stores a position and a weight
Parametric uses integer encoding while particles require 64-bit floating-point precision per sample
Particle filters redundantly store the full sensor history for each particle to allow reprocessing
Parametric stores one matrix per sensor axis while particles require one full vector per sensor
jsonData.explanation: Parametric: two float values (mean μ and variance σ²) ≈ 16 bytes. Non-parametric: ~10,000 particles × (x position + weight) ≈ 160,000 bytes — a 10,000× difference. The trade-off is flexibility: particles can model any shape while parameters only model single-peaked Gaussian distributions.

jsonData.question: Why does receiving a new sensor measurement (the correction step) reduce the robot's positional uncertainty?
options: Because the robot pauses all motion during sensing, preventing actuator noise from accumulating further
Because sensor evidence concentrates probability mass around positions consistent with the measurement
Because the Gaussian distribution automatically narrows as more time passes after the last prediction
Because sensor readings overwrite the prior belief entirely and replace it with one precise position
jsonData.explanation: Sensor evidence acts as a filter: positions whose predicted sensor output matches the actual measurement become more probable; inconsistent positions become less probable. This concentrates the distribution (reduces variance). The correction does NOT overwrite the prior — it multiplies it by the likelihood P(z|x).

jsonData.question: Using the lecture scenario (P(N)=0.5, P(F)=0.5, P(z=2|N)=0.8, P(z=2|F)=0.2, P(z)=0.5), what is P(Far | z=2)?
options: 0.5 — the prior probability of being far from the wall before any sensing occurred
0.4 — the joint probability P(z=2 AND Near) before applying the normalization step
0.8 — the sensor likelihood P(z=2|Near) incorrectly assigned to the Far hypothesis
jsonData.explanation: P(F|z) = P(z|F) × P(F) / P(z) = (0.2 × 0.5) / 0.5 = 0.1/0.5 = 0.2. After observing z=2m, Far drops from prior 0.5 to posterior 0.2, while Near rises to 0.8. Verification: P(N|z) + P(F|z) = 0.8 + 0.2 = 1.0 ✓. Option B is the Near joint probability, not the Far posterior.

jsonData.question: The Bayes Filter cycle of prediction and correction steps is described in the lecture as the core of which robotics applications?
options: Robot path planning and real-time obstacle avoidance in dynamic environments
Object recognition and semantic scene understanding via deep learning cameras
Task scheduling and resource allocation across distributed multi-robot teams
Robot localization and SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping)
jsonData.explanation: The lecture explicitly states: prediction + correction 'form the Bayes Filter cycle used in robot localization and SLAM.' Localization = knowing where the robot is; SLAM = simultaneously building a map while tracking position. Both depend on this recursive Bayesian estimation cycle.

jsonData.question: Which of the following best contrasts deterministic and probabilistic robot programming?
options: Deterministic outputs exact values and ignores all uncertainty; probabilistic represents it as distributions
Deterministic is more computationally complex; probabilistic is simpler but significantly less reliable
Deterministic works well in real-world environments; probabilistic is mainly useful for simulation
Deterministic programs require Gaussian noise models internally; probabilistic programs use only discrete states
jsonData.explanation: The comparison table from the lecture: Deterministic — exact value output, uncertainty ignored, limited real-world use, low complexity. Probabilistic — distribution output, uncertainty modeled, essential for real-world robotics, higher complexity. Options B and C reverse the real-world applicability comparison.

jsonData.question: A LIDAR sensor reads a wall at 5.2m when the true distance is 5.0m. How is this classified in the lecture's uncertainty framework?
options: A catastrophic sensor failure indicating the LIDAR hardware needs immediate recalibration or replacement
Normal sensor noise (~4% error) that probabilistic models handle by maintaining an uncertainty distribution
A model inaccuracy because the motion model does not correctly predict wall positions over time
An environmental change, because the wall must have shifted slightly since the map was built
jsonData.explanation: Sensor noise = 'The Eyes Lie.' LIDAR naturally reads 5.2m when the wall is at 5.0m — a 4% error within the expected ±2-5% range. The lecture uses smartphone GPS (3-5 meter errors) as a relatable example. This is completely normal, expected behavior — not a failure. Probabilistic models assume and handle this.

jsonData.question: Parametric belief representation (using μ and σ²) fails to correctly model robot uncertainty when:
options: The robot is moving faster than the Gaussian distribution can dynamically adapt to accurately track its changing position
New sensor readings arrive more frequently than Bayesian update computations can complete in real-time
The robot's true uncertainty is multimodal, such as when identical landmarks make localization ambiguous
The variance σ² becomes numerically larger than the mean μ in the Gaussian distribution parameters
jsonData.explanation: Parametric representation assumes a single-peaked Gaussian (unimodal). When the robot is near identical landmarks (e.g., identical doors), the true belief has multiple equal-probability peaks. A single μ and σ² cannot represent multiple peaks — it would collapse them into one incorrect Gaussian blob.

jsonData.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Bayesian belief update process?
options: Compute the posterior first using guessed evidence, then retroactively establish the prior belief from history
Establish prior → compute posterior first → then collect evidence → then apply likelihood
Apply likelihood directly → observe evidence → establish prior last → compute posterior
Establish prior → observe new evidence → apply likelihood → compute posterior
jsonData.explanation: The four-step Bayesian process: (1) start with prior P(A) — initial belief, (2) observe evidence B from sensors, (3) apply likelihood P(B|A) — how consistent is this evidence with each hypothesis, (4) compute posterior P(A|B) via Bayes' Rule. This sequence cannot be reordered without breaking the mathematical derivation.

jsonData.question: A robot commanded to move 1 meter actually moves 0.95 meters due to wheel slippage. This 5% error is classified as which type of uncertainty?
options: Actuator noise — the motor and wheel system failed to execute the motion command with full accuracy
Sensor noise — the position measurement after movement reported an incorrect final distance
Model inaccuracy — the position = velocity × time formula did not account for all physical factors
Environmental change — the floor surface conditions have dynamically altered the expected travel distance throughout the route
jsonData.explanation: Actuator noise = 'The Muscles Fail.' The robot commanded 1m but moved 0.95m due to wheel slippage. This is a direct execution error — the actuator (motor + wheel system) imperfectly carried out the command. This is distinct from sensor noise, which would be inaccurately measuring the 0.95m that actually occurred.

jsonData.question: A robot must localize itself in real-time inside a well-mapped static building where uncertainty is expected to be unimodal and Gaussian. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Parametric representation (μ, σ²) — efficient, fast, and fully correct when uncertainty is Gaussian
Particle filter with 1,000 particles as a lightweight non-parametric approach for general scenarios
Particle filter with 10,000 particles — the only reliable way to guarantee accurate position tracking
Uniform distribution — unimodal uncertainty cannot be safely assumed without formal verification
jsonData.explanation: When the belief is unimodal (single-peaked Gaussian), parametric representation is ideal: ~16 bytes, very fast computation, perfectly accurate for this case. A particle filter with 10,000 particles uses ~160,000 bytes and is ~10,000× more expensive computationally — with no benefit when the Gaussian assumption holds.

jsonData.question: According to the lecture's walking analogy for the Markov Property, what information does a person need to decide their very next step toward a destination?
options: The full history of every step previously taken, to avoid accidentally retracing any path
Only the final destination address, with no knowledge of current position required
Only their current position and their intended direction of travel
Current position, the path taken so far, and locations of all previously encountered obstacles
jsonData.explanation: The Markov walking analogy: you only need your current position and intended direction — NOT the full history of past steps. This maps directly to P(xt | xt-1, ut): the next state requires only the current state and the current action. The entire past history beyond the current state is irrelevant.

jsonData.question: A robot successfully navigates a hospital hallway at 8:00 AM. By 8:03 AM, the same navigation program fails. Which uncertainty source is primarily responsible?
options: Sensor noise, because extended LIDAR operation causes thermal drift that degrades measurement accuracy over time
Actuator noise, because wheel motors heat up during operation and gradually lose rotational precision
Model inaccuracy, because the simplified motion model accumulates compounding error over three minutes
Environmental changes — the hallway now has nurses with carts, an open door, and children blocking the path
jsonData.explanation: The lecture's hospital hallway scenario explicitly illustrates environmental changes: 8:00 clear path, 8:01 nurse with cart, 8:02 door opens, 8:03 children running. 'The World is Alive.' A static map becomes invalid as the environment changes. The other sources are constant, not event-triggered at specific times.

jsonData.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as an application of Bayes' Rule in the lecture's robotics applications section?
options: Robot path planning and trajectory optimization for obstacle avoidance
Robot localization (updating beliefs about the robot's position from sensor data)
Sensor fusion (combining information from multiple different sensors)
Mapping (updating beliefs about obstacle locations in the environment)
jsonData.explanation: The lecture explicitly lists four Bayes' Rule applications: (1) Robot Localization, (2) Mapping, (3) Sensor Fusion, and (4) Robot Learning (updating model parameters from observations). Path planning is a separate robotics subfield not listed as a Bayesian inference application in this lecture.

jsonData.question: A robot enters a completely unknown environment with no prior map data. Which probability distribution should represent its initial position belief?
options: Gaussian distribution centered at the starting coordinates with an appropriately large variance
Uniform distribution, since no position is more probable than any other without prior data
Multimodal distribution with peaks at all recognizable landmark positions seen at startup
A single narrow peak (delta function) at the physical origin of the robot's coordinate frame
jsonData.explanation: With zero prior information, every position is equally likely — a uniform distribution assigns equal probability everywhere. A Gaussian centered at the start point incorrectly assumes the robot is probably near that point. A delta function implies perfect knowledge. Sensing then updates the uniform prior via Bayes' Rule.

jsonData.question: After a robot executes a motion command, its position belief distribution has the same central estimate but a noticeably larger variance. What causes this widening?
options: The sensor model incorrectly merges two successive Gaussian distributions into one wider combined curve
The normalization term P(B) in Bayes' Rule increases proportionally during the prediction step computation
Actuator noise adds uncertainty to the prior distribution when the robot executes the motion command
The Markov Assumption forces the robot to discard all sensor measurements recorded prior to the motion
jsonData.explanation: In the prediction step, the motion model is combined with a noise model (actuator uncertainty). This mathematically adds variance: the distribution widens to represent possible outcomes from Shelf 5.8 to 6.3, caused by wheel slip and motor variation. The Markov Assumption is about memory, not about distribution shape.

jsonData.question: A warehouse robot must localize near several identical crates. Both a Kalman Filter (parametric) and a Particle Filter (non-parametric) are available. Which is the correct choice and reasoning?
options: Kalman Filter, because it can represent multimodal uncertainty about crate positions more accurately
Kalman Filter, because particles cannot adequately approximate Gaussian sensor noise distributions
Particle Filter only if there are more than 100 crates; use Kalman Filter for fewer crates
Particle Filter — identical crates create multimodal belief that the Kalman Filter's Gaussian assumption cannot represent
jsonData.explanation: Identical crates cause multimodal uncertainty — the robot could be near any crate with equal probability. The Kalman Filter assumes a unimodal Gaussian belief; it cannot represent multiple peaks and would produce an incorrect single-center estimate. The Particle Filter handles any distribution shape, making it correct for this ambiguous scenario.

quizzes.name: lec2: Sensors, Signals, and Data Processing

jsonData.question: Which statement best captures the CS philosophy about sensors stated in this lecture?
options: Sensors provide accurate data that can be used directly by the control system without modification
Software must filter, calibrate, and fuse sensor lies to build a reliable model of the world
Sensors always output digital data representing physical quantities accurately after conversion
Hardware engineers are fully responsible for correcting all sensor errors before data reaches software
jsonData.explanation: The lecture explicitly states: 'All sensors lie. The job of the software is to filter, calibrate, and combine these lies into a reliable model of the world.' Sensors only know voltage; extracting meaning is the software's responsibility. Options A and C incorrectly suggest sensors are inherently accurate, and D misattributes the calibration responsibility to EE rather than CS.

jsonData.question: According to the Nyquist-Shannon Theorem, which condition must the sampling frequency $f_s$ satisfy to avoid aliasing?
options: $f_s > 2 f_{max}$
$f_s = f_{max}$
$f_s < 2 f_{max}$
$f_s \geq f_{max}$
jsonData.explanation: The Nyquist-Shannon Theorem requires $f_s > 2 f_{max}$, where $f_{max}$ is the highest frequency in the signal. Sampling at exactly $f_{max}$ (option B) is the worst case — it produces aliasing as shown in the lecture's vibration example where all samples return zero.

jsonData.question: In signal processing for robotics, aliasing is best described as:
options: A sensor calibrated incorrectly, introducing a systematic constant offset in all readings
A filter that introduces excessive delay between input and filtered output
Under-sampling that causes a signal to appear as a false frequency or vanish entirely
Sensor internal noise accumulating and permanently corrupting the measurement signal output
jsonData.explanation: Aliasing occurs when the sampling rate is too low relative to the signal frequency, causing the true signal to appear as a lower-frequency false signal, or to disappear entirely. The lecture demonstrates this with a 100 Hz vibration sampled at 100 Hz, producing all-zero readings — not because there is no motion, but because the same phase is always sampled. Option A describes bias, option D describes noise accumulation.

jsonData.question: Which statement correctly describes the computational complexity of a circular (ring) buffer used for sensor buffering?
options: O(N) insertion and O(1) memory — insertion is linear in window size
O(1) memory and O(N) insertion — memory is constant but insertion scales with N
O(log N) insertion and O(N) memory — tree-based indexing reduces insertion cost
O(1) insertion and O(N) memory — constant-time insertion with fixed-size storage
jsonData.explanation: A circular buffer has O(1) insertion and removal (the head and tail pointers simply advance) and uses O(N) fixed memory where N is the buffer capacity. Old data is overwritten automatically. Options A and B have insertion and memory complexities swapped. This makes circular buffers ideal for bridging the rate mismatch between a 1000 Hz sensor and a 100 Hz control loop.

jsonData.question: In the sensor-to-software pipeline, what is the primary function of a transducer?
options: Converting a physical phenomenon into an electrical voltage signal
Digitizing a continuous analog voltage into discrete binary integer values
Storing raw sensor readings in memory for CPU batch processing
Filtering electrical noise from the analog signal before it reaches the ADC
jsonData.explanation: A transducer converts physical phenomena (heat, light, acceleration, pressure) into a voltage signal. This is an EE responsibility (circuit design). Digitization is performed by the ADC (option B), filtering is a software or analog EE task (option D), and storage is handled by memory systems (option C).

jsonData.question: Why is the arithmetic averaging method effective at reducing Gaussian (white) noise in sensor readings?
options: Gaussian noise is hardware-generated, so averaging corrects it by shifting the signal baseline
Gaussian noise is periodic, so averaging removes its repeating cyclic pattern over time
Its zero mean makes positive and negative errors cancel over many samples
Averaging increases the sampling rate, which directly lowers the noise floor level
jsonData.explanation: Gaussian noise has zero mean, meaning random positive and negative deviations cancel when summed across many samples, making the average converge to the true value. The lecture demonstrates this: 10 samples with zero-mean noise average to exactly 5.0. When noise is NOT zero-mean (as in the second example, mean = 0.1), averaging gives 5.1 — a systematic overestimate, not the true value.

jsonData.question: In the sensor-to-software pipeline, the CS engineer's key responsibility at the ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter) stage is:
options: Designing the analog circuit amplification to boost the voltage signal strength
Understanding the resolution limits introduced by quantization
Selecting appropriate electromagnetic shielding to protect the signal from interference
Configuring the physical transducer sensitivity for the target measurement phenomenon
jsonData.explanation: At the ADC stage, the CS responsibility is understanding resolution limits — for example, knowing that a 10-bit ADC has 1024 steps and a step size of 4.88 mV at 5V reference. Amplification and shielding (options A and C) are EE responsibilities. Transducer sensitivity (option D) is a physics and EE concern at the physical phenomenon stage.

jsonData.question: Why is the low-pass filter described in this lecture called an 'Exponential Moving Average (EMA)'?
options: The filter coefficient α grows exponentially with the number of samples in the window
The filter uses an exponential function in its continuous-time frequency-domain transfer equation
The filter's computational time complexity is exponential in the number of samples processed
Older measurements receive exponentially decreasing weight in the final filtered output
jsonData.explanation: When the EMA recursion $y_k = \alpha z_k + (1-\alpha)y_{k-1}$ is expanded, it equals $\alpha z_k + \alpha(1-\alpha)z_{k-1} + \alpha(1-\alpha)^2 z_{k-2} + \ldots$ — each past measurement is multiplied by $(1-\alpha)^n$, which decays exponentially. The most recent sample has weight $\alpha$, the previous has $\alpha(1-\alpha)$, and so on. Options A, B, and C all misidentify where the 'exponential' arises.

jsonData.question: A robot's gyroscope develops persistent drift (bias instability). The lecture describes three fixes. Which is labeled the BEST solution?
options: Use sensor fusion with an absolute reference such as GPS or accelerometer
Apply a moving average filter to smooth out the slowly drifting bias over many samples
Increase the gyroscope sampling rate to capture the slowly changing bias more accurately
Apply a high-pass filter to remove the low-frequency drift component from the signal
jsonData.explanation: The lecture explicitly labels sensor fusion (e.g., Gyro + Accelerometer via a complementary filter, or IMU + GPS) as the 'Best Solution' for drift. Averaging (option B) cannot fix a systematic drift since the noise is not zero-mean. A high-pass filter (option D) removes slow components but discards real slow motion too, and higher sampling rate (option C) does not address the root cause of bias drift.

jsonData.question: An IMU reads [9.80, 9.82, 47.00, 9.79, 9.81] m/s². Computing the arithmetic mean gives 17.24 m/s². Why does averaging fail here?
options: Averaging only works within a predefined minimum and maximum sensor value range
A single extreme outlier disproportionately inflates the computed mean, corrupting the result
Averaging is only effective for noise that follows a perfectly uniform statistical distribution
The averaging window must be cleared after each detected spike before new estimates stabilize
jsonData.explanation: The 47.00 spike is impulse (salt-and-pepper) noise. Because the mean is sensitive to every value's magnitude, one extreme value pulls the result far from the true signal (~9.81). This is exactly why the median filter is preferred for impulse noise — the median of [9.79, 9.80, 9.81, 9.82, 47.00] is 9.81, unaffected by the spike's magnitude.

jsonData.question: If a robot's IMU samples at $f_s = 500$ Hz, what is the sampling period $T_s$?
jsonData.explanation: $T_s = 1/f_s = 1/500 = 0.002$ s (2 milliseconds per sample). Option B (0.02 s) corresponds to 50 Hz sampling, option D (0.5 s) to 2 Hz. This relationship $T_s = 1/f_s$ is fundamental to all sampling-rate calculations in the lecture's Nyquist analysis.

jsonData.question: A low-pass EMA filter uses α = 0.1. Given $y_{k-1} = 10.0$ and $z_k = 20.0$, what is the new filtered output $y_k$?
jsonData.explanation: $y_k = \alpha z_k + (1-\alpha)y_{k-1} = 0.1 \times 20 + 0.9 \times 10 = 2.0 + 9.0 = 11.0$. Option A (15.0) is a simple unweighted average. Option C (2.0) applies only the $\alpha z_k$ term. With α = 0.1, the filter trusts the history 90% and the new reading only 10%, resulting in very slow adaptation — which is the expected behavior for small α.

jsonData.question: A sonar sensor on a mobile robot occasionally produces extreme spike values (e.g., 500 m when the true range is ~2 m). Which filter should be applied to remove these outliers?
options: Median filter
Moving average filter
High-pass filter
Exponential moving average filter
jsonData.explanation: The median filter is the correct choice for salt-and-pepper (impulse) noise. It selects the middle value after sorting, so the spike's magnitude does not affect the result. The moving average (option B) and EMA (option D) both compute weighted means — one extreme value corrupts them, as demonstrated in the lecture: (9.8 + 9.82 + 47 + 9.79 + 9.81)/5 = 17.24, which is completely wrong.

jsonData.question: Which data format does LIDAR produce, and what is its key software challenge?
options: Scalar — each scan returns a single aggregate distance to the nearest obstacle
Point cloud (N vectors) — the number of points varies per scan, making allocation non-trivial
Matrix — LIDAR produces a fixed-size 2D array of distance values at every time step
3D vector — LIDAR measures exactly x, y, and z coordinates for a single target point
jsonData.explanation: LIDAR generates point clouds — collections of N distance vectors — where N is not fixed between scans. This variable size is the key software challenge highlighted in the lecture. Cameras produce matrices (option C, fixed 640×480 pixels). Accelerometers and gyroscopes produce 3-value vectors (option D). Temperature sensors produce scalars (option A).

jsonData.question: A moving average filter uses a window size of N = 10. After a sudden step change in the input signal, approximately how many samples are needed to reach 50% of the new true value?
options: 10 samples
1 sample
5 samples
20 samples
jsonData.explanation: The phase lag of a moving average is approximately N/2 samples. With N = 10, the output reaches ~50% of a step input after ~5 samples. The lecture demonstrates this: with N = 4 and input [0,0,0,10,10,10,10], the output is [0,0,0,2.5,5,7.5,10] — reaching 5 (50% of 10) at sample 5, which is N/2 = 2 samples after the step at sample 4.

jsonData.question: A wheel encoder reports 0.95 m for a true 1.0 m move and has a known bias of 0.05 m. Using the full calibration formula $X_{cal} = (X_{raw} - b) \cdot s$ where $s = 1.0/0.95 \approx 1.0526$, what is the corrected reading?
jsonData.explanation: $(X_{raw} - b) \cdot s = (0.95 - 0.05) \times 1.0526 = 0.90 \times 1.0526 \approx 0.947$ m. Option A (0.950) applies scale without bias removal. Option B (0.900) applies bias only without scaling. Option D (1.000) is the true value, not the calibrated reading — the lecture shows bias+scale combined still leaves a small residual, which is why neither correction alone is sufficient.

jsonData.question: A mobile robot needs camera video streaming at 60 fps generating megabytes of data per second. Which data acquisition method should be used?
options: Polling, because cameras have fixed frame rates making periodic checks efficient and predictable
Interrupt-Driven I/O, because each completed frame triggers a hardware interrupt to the CPU
Polling or Interrupt equally, because the camera frame rate determines the required CPU rate
DMA (Direct Memory Access), because it transfers frame data without CPU involvement
jsonData.explanation: DMA is the correct choice for cameras because they generate megabytes per second — far too much for the CPU to handle with polling (wasted cycles) or interrupts (ISR overhead per byte). DMA transfers data directly between the camera peripheral and memory; the CPU only sets up DMA once and gets notified when a full frame is ready. The lecture explicitly lists 'Cameras → DMA' in the robotics perspective table.

jsonData.question: A stationary robot's gyroscope outputs: 0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.05, 0.08 rad/s over 5 seconds. What type of noise is this, and what is the key danger?
options: Salt-and-pepper noise — spikes corrupt individual readings but the long-term mean remains accurate
Drift (bias instability) — readings accumulate into a large orientation error over time
Gaussian noise — the average will converge toward zero, giving an accurate long-term orientation
Quantization noise — fixed ADC step sizes create discrete jumps in the reported angular value
jsonData.explanation: The monotonically increasing values indicate drift (bias instability) — the gyro 'zero' is slowly shifting. Unlike Gaussian noise (which averages out), drift is systematic and non-zero-mean. Integrating 0.1 rad/s over 10 s gives 1.0 rad of orientation error even though the robot never moved. The lecture warns this corrupts EKF and SLAM state estimation.

jsonData.question: A position sensor has noise of ±1 mm and samples at 100 Hz (Δt = 0.01 s). What velocity noise magnitude results from directly applying numerical differentiation to the raw position data?
options: ±1 mm/s
±10 mm/s
jsonData.explanation: $v_{noise} = \Delta x_{noise} / \Delta t = 0.001 \text{ m} / 0.01 \text{ s} = 0.1 \text{ m/s}$. A 1 mm position noise becomes 0.1 m/s velocity noise — large enough to make a stationary robot appear to be violently shaking. This is why the lecture's golden rule states: 'Never differentiate raw sensor data. Filter first, then differentiate.'

jsonData.question: A robot needs real-time wheel velocity filtering for a PID loop at 500 Hz. Memory is limited to O(1). Which filter is most appropriate?
options: Moving average with a large window for maximum Gaussian noise reduction
Median filter to reject velocity outlier spikes in the real-time stream
High-pass filter to remove the constant DC component from the velocity reading
Low-pass EMA filter with tunable α and O(1) memory
jsonData.explanation: EMA requires only O(1) memory (just two variables: previous output and α), runs in O(1) per sample, is tunable for the noise/responsiveness tradeoff via α, and is listed in the lecture as the standard choice for 'IMU, wheel velocity, real-time control.' Moving average (option A) requires O(N) memory and introduces phase lag. Median filter (option B) requires O(N) sorted storage. HPF (option C) removes DC but amplifies noise.

jsonData.question: In the complementary filter formula $\theta_k = \alpha(\theta_{k-1} + \omega \Delta t) + (1-\alpha)\theta_{accel}$, what does the value of $\alpha$ control?
options: The relative trust weight between the gyroscope prediction and the accelerometer correction
The sampling rate ratio required between the IMU and the complementary filter update loop
The maximum allowable tilt angle before the filter flags a potential sensor failure condition
The cut-off frequency of the low-pass component applied internally to the accelerometer signal
jsonData.explanation: α directly controls how much the filter trusts the gyroscope vs. the accelerometer. With α ≈ 0.97, the filter uses 97% gyroscope data (fast, smooth, but drifts) and 3% accelerometer data (slow, noisy, but drift-free). The lecture's example uses this value specifically because gyroscopes are much more responsive than accelerometers, but need long-term correction.

jsonData.question: A robot engineer classifies wheel encoders as 'proprioceptive' and LIDAR as 'exteroceptive.' What is the key distinguishing characteristic?
options: Proprioceptive sensors sample at kHz rates while exteroceptive sensors operate at Hz rates
Proprioceptive sensors measure the robot's internal state; exteroceptive sensors sense the external environment
Proprioceptive sensors output scalar data while exteroceptive sensors produce vectors or matrices
Proprioceptive sensors are calibrated with bias correction while exteroceptive sensors use scale factors
jsonData.explanation: Proprioceptive sensors measure the robot's own internal state (encoders → odometry/velocity, IMU → orientation, current sensor → stall detection). Exteroceptive sensors measure the external world (LIDAR → mapping, camera → vision, microphone → audio events). Rate and data format (options A and C) vary within each category and do not define the classification.

jsonData.question: What is the key difference in CPU usage between polling and interrupt-driven I/O for sensor acquisition?
options: Polling requires dedicated hardware peripherals while interrupts work on any CPU architecture
Interrupts always consume more CPU than polling because they require register save/restore overhead
Polling wastes CPU by constantly checking for data; interrupts free the CPU to work between events
Polling is more CPU-efficient for high-speed sensors while interrupts suit only slow sensors
jsonData.explanation: Polling keeps the CPU in a busy-wait loop continuously checking a status register, wasting all cycles on checking. With interrupt-driven I/O, the CPU executes its main task and only stops for the ISR when a data-ready signal arrives — the lecture rates polling as 'High CPU Usage' and interrupts as 'Medium.' Option B is incorrect: ISR register overhead is small and bounded, far less than polling's continuous waste.

jsonData.question: What is the memory complexity difference between the Moving Average filter and the Exponential Moving Average (EMA) filter?
options: EMA requires O(N) memory to track its exponentially weighted history; Moving Average uses O(1)
Both require O(N) memory, but EMA distributes computation across multiple forward and backward passes
Both require O(1) memory, but Moving Average sorts values internally, increasing time complexity
Moving Average requires O(N) memory to store the sample window; EMA requires only O(1) memory
jsonData.explanation: Moving Average must store the last N raw samples in a circular buffer to compute the sliding window mean — O(N) memory. EMA only needs two values: the previous filtered output $y_{k-1}$ and the parameter α — O(1) memory. This is why the lecture's comparison table shows EMA as the choice when memory is constrained, and why it suits embedded real-time systems.

jsonData.question: Why does arithmetic averaging (mean) effectively reduce Gaussian noise but fail to correct sensor drift?
options: Averaging cancels zero-mean random fluctuations but cannot eliminate a systematic, slowly shifting bias
Drift is removed by averaging over a sufficiently large window; the window is simply too small in practice
Gaussian noise has a non-zero mean while drift has zero mean, so averaging only applies to drift
Averaging is only valid for periodic signals, and neither Gaussian noise nor drift is periodic
jsonData.explanation: Gaussian noise has zero mean, so positive and negative deviations cancel over many samples. Drift is a slowly growing systematic offset — its mean is non-zero and increasing. Averaging many drifted readings does not return the true value; it returns the true value plus the average drift. This is why drift requires sensor fusion or periodic recalibration, not averaging. Option C has the mean properties reversed.

jsonData.question: LIDAR readings for a single scan direction are [2.1, 2.0, 2.2, 150.0, 2.1] meters. The mean is 31.68 m; the median is 2.1 m. What does this illustrate about median vs. mean filtering?
options: Median filtering requires sorting at each step, making it computationally slower in all scenarios
Median depends on value order, not magnitude, making it robust to extreme outliers that distort the mean
The mean is more accurate for LIDAR because it integrates all available sensor range information
Median filters are preferred because they require less memory than window-based mean filters
jsonData.explanation: The median only cares about whether a value is above or below the midpoint — 150.0 is simply 'the largest,' ranked 5th of 5. Even if the spike were 1,000,000 m, the median stays 2.1 m. The mean, however, is pulled to 31.68 m because it weighs every value by magnitude. The lecture states: 'The median depends only on order, not magnitude. That makes it extremely robust.'

jsonData.question: The high-pass filter formula is $y_k = \alpha(y_{k-1} + z_k - z_{k-1})$. What happens to the output when the input $z_k$ is perfectly constant for many steps?
options: The output equals the constant value, since the filter tracks and follows the current signal level
The output oscillates around the constant value with decreasing amplitude over time
The output decays to zero, because the difference term $(z_k - z_{k-1})$ becomes zero for a constant input
The output remains at its initial value, since the filter preserves prior state indefinitely
jsonData.explanation: When $z_k = z_{k-1}$ (constant input), the difference $(z_k - z_{k-1}) = 0$, so $y_k = \alpha \cdot y_{k-1}$. With $\alpha < 1$, this geometric decay drives $y_k \to 0$ over time — constant signals disappear. This is precisely the defining behavior of a high-pass filter: it blocks DC (constant) components and passes only changes. This is used to remove gravity from accelerometer data: $a_{total} = a_{motion} + g$; HPF removes the constant $g$.

jsonData.question: A robot vibrates at exactly 100 Hz and the IMU samples at exactly 100 Hz. The vibration signal is $x(t) = A\sin(2\pi \cdot 100t)$. What do the IMU measurements look like, and why?
options: Full vibration amplitude — sampling at the signal's own frequency always captures its peak values
Random noise — equal-frequency sampling hits random phases of the sinusoidal vibration
A lower-frequency oscillation — the wagon-wheel aliasing effect creates a false backward frequency
A constant value near zero — each sample hits exactly the same phase of the wave every period
jsonData.explanation: At $t = 0.01$ s: $\sin(2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 0.01) = \sin(2\pi) = 0$. At $t = 0.02$ s: $\sin(4\pi) = 0$. Every sample hits an integer multiple of $2\pi$, always returning zero. The real vibration is invisible — the IMU appears to see no motion at all. This is a catastrophic aliasing case that corrupts EKF and SLAM state estimation by making the filter treat real vibration as zero acceleration.

jsonData.question: A wheel encoder has both a bias of b = 0.05 m and a scale error (reads 0.95 m for true 1.0 m). If ONLY bias correction is applied ($X_{cal} = X_{raw} - b$), what residual problem remains?
options: Proportional (scale) error persists — the sensor still underestimates distances after offset removal
Bias correction overcorrects, making the sensor systematically overestimate true distances
Without scale correction, the bias correction itself becomes numerically unstable over time
Bias correction removes the offset, leaving only random Gaussian noise as the remaining error
jsonData.explanation: After bias-only correction: $X_{cal} = 0.95 - 0.05 = 0.90$ m versus the true 1.0 m — a 10% underestimate. The scale error (sensor reads 95% of true distance) is untouched. The lecture's table confirms: bias-only → 'proportional error remains.' Only the combined formula $X_{cal} = (X_{raw} - b) \cdot s$ addresses both. Option D incorrectly suggests averaging would fix it.

jsonData.question: Why does operating an IMU at the same frequency as motor vibration (~100 Hz) corrupt state estimation algorithms like EKF and SLAM?
options: The IMU's ADC saturates at the vibration frequency, clipping legitimate motion readings entirely
Aliased vibration looks identical to real acceleration, so EKF interprets noise as genuine motion
IMUs at low sampling rates consume excessive memory bandwidth, slowing SLAM computation
EKF requires at least 10x oversampling relative to motor vibration regardless of frequency
jsonData.explanation: When IMU sampling equals vibration frequency, aliasing makes the vibration appear as a false signal (or disappear and reappear erratically). EKF cannot distinguish this from real acceleration — the filter updates pose based on noise, leading to drift, false pose updates, and unstable control. The lecture emphasizes: 'You cannot distinguish vibration from real acceleration,' corrupting both EKF and SLAM.

jsonData.question: What is the critical difference between static calibration and dynamic calibration (auto-zeroing)?
options: Static calibration applies both bias and scale correction; dynamic calibration updates only scale factor
Dynamic calibration uses sensor fusion while static calibration uses only mathematical correction formulas
Static calibration is one-time; dynamic calibration automatically updates bias estimates during operation
Static calibration is done by hardware engineers; dynamic calibration is implemented in robot firmware only
jsonData.explanation: Static calibration is performed once before deployment (e.g., measure bias at startup). Dynamic calibration (auto-zeroing) continuously updates the bias estimate while the robot operates — but only when the robot is confirmed to be stationary. The lecture warns: 'If you calibrate while moving, you will calibrate out the actual motion.' Options A, B, and D describe incorrect distinctions.

jsonData.question: A submarine robot's pressure sensor outputs exactly 47.3 kPa for 500 consecutive samples with zero variance. What does this indicate, and how should it be detected?
options: This is expected Gaussian behavior — real sensors frequently output identical values for extended periods
The sensor is working correctly since underwater pressure changes are inherently very slow and stable
The sensor is saturated at its maximum value, detectable via a value range limit check
The sensor is likely frozen or malfunctioning, detectable through a near-zero variance check
jsonData.explanation: Real sensors always have some thermal noise and ADC quantization variation — perfect constancy is physically impossible. The lecture states: 'If variance ≈ 0 → suspicious.' This is the 'Stuck Detector' pattern for sensor diagnostics. Zero variance over 500 samples strongly indicates the sensor is frozen (stuck output), disconnected, or returning a cached value. Option C describes saturation detection, which is a different diagnostic.

jsonData.question: A robot's GPS reports a 0.5 m position jump within one 10 ms sample period, but the robot's maximum speed is 1 m/s. How should the software respond?
options: Reject it as an outlier — the position change violates the robot's known physical speed limit
Accept it, since GPS systems can report position changes faster than the robot physically moves
Average it with the previous 5 GPS readings to reduce its impact on the position estimate
Recalibrate the GPS scale factor, since the reading indicates a systematic proportional error
jsonData.explanation: Rate limit check: $\Delta x_{max} = v_{max} \cdot \Delta t = 1 \cdot 0.01 = 0.01$ m per sample. A jump of 0.5 m is 50× the physical limit — physically impossible. The lecture's outlier detection principle: 'Physics is a constraint. Use it. Sensors can lie, physics does not.' The reading must be rejected. Averaging (option C) would reduce but not eliminate its effect on the position estimate.

jsonData.question: According to the practical robotics noise mapping in the lecture, which sensor exhibits BOTH Gaussian noise AND drift (bias instability)?
options: IMU accelerometer — which primarily exhibits only Gaussian noise from thermal electron motion
IMU gyroscope — which exhibits Gaussian noise combined with drift (bias instability) over time
Magnetometer — which exhibits drift combined with external magnetic field disturbances
Wheel encoders — which exhibit quantization noise combined with occasional impulse noise
jsonData.explanation: The lecture's noise mapping table explicitly assigns 'Gaussian + Drift' to the IMU gyroscope. This dual problem is why gyroscopes require both low-pass filtering (for Gaussian) and sensor fusion or recalibration (for drift). The accelerometer has Gaussian only. The magnetometer has Drift + Disturbance. Encoders have Quantization + Impulse.

jsonData.question: A temperature sensor updates at 1 Hz with smooth, slowly varying readings. A student proposes applying a median filter with N = 5. What is the best assessment of this choice?
options: Median filter requires O(N) memory, which is prohibitively expensive for any embedded 1 Hz application
The median filter cannot handle the high variability expected from temperature sensor readings
Median's outlier-rejection is unnecessary here; a simpler moving average or EMA is more appropriate
Median filtering introduces an N/2 phase lag that is unacceptable for any safety-critical temperature monitoring
jsonData.explanation: The lecture maps temperature sensors to polling + simple filtering (moving average). Median filters are designed for impulse/spike noise (LIDAR, ultrasonic, touch sensors). A slow, smooth temperature signal at 1 Hz has no such spikes — applying a median filter adds sorting overhead and O(N) memory with no benefit. A moving average or EMA achieves the same smoothing more efficiently. Option D's phase lag concern is valid but secondary to the wrong tool choice.

jsonData.question: A navigation system requires IMU data at 2 kHz for high-precision state estimation. Which acquisition method should be used?
options: Polling, because the CPU can check the IMU status register every 0.5 ms in a tight busy-wait loop
Interrupt-Driven I/O, since the IMU asserts a data-ready pin and triggers a hardware interrupt per sample
Interrupt + polling hybrid, using DMA for first-stage buffering and polling for overflow detection
DMA, because CPU-free transfers prevent interrupt latency from corrupting high-rate timing
jsonData.explanation: The lecture's table: 'IMU at very high speed (>1 kHz) → DMA.' At 2 kHz, an interrupt fires every 0.5 ms — the ISR overhead and latency jitter would corrupt the precise timing needed for state estimation. DMA transfers each sample directly to memory with deterministic timing and zero CPU cycles during transfer. Polling (option A) would consume the CPU entirely. Option B (interrupt at 2 kHz) introduces unacceptable ISR overhead.

jsonData.question: A mobile robot's gyroscope-based orientation estimate drifts significantly after several minutes of operation. What is the most effective long-term solution?
options: Use sensor fusion with an absolute reference (e.g., accelerometer or GPS) to correct long-term drift
Increase the gyroscope sampling rate from 100 Hz to 1 kHz to reduce cumulative integration error
Apply a high-pass filter to remove the slowly drifting bias from the gyroscope angular velocity
Reset the gyroscope bias estimate to zero at fixed time intervals independent of robot motion state
jsonData.explanation: The lecture labels sensor fusion (complementary filter with accelerometer, or IMU + GPS) as the 'Best Solution' for drift. Higher sampling rate (option B) doesn't reduce bias drift — it only improves resolution. A high-pass filter (option C) removes slow drift but also removes real slow rotations. Resetting bias at fixed intervals (option D) is dangerous: if the robot is moving during the reset, real motion gets calibrated out.

jsonData.question: According to the lecture's conceptual flow (Reality → Measurement Model → Probability Model → Estimator → Code), what must be determined BEFORE writing any filtering or estimation code?
options: The programming language and memory model best suited for the embedded hardware platform
The optimality criterion (MMSE, ML, or MAP) — what 'best estimate' actually means mathematically
The specific hardware interrupt vector assignments for each connected sensor peripheral
The sampling rate and buffer size required to store exactly one second of raw sensor readings
jsonData.explanation: The lecture states: 'Before writing any code, we must answer: What are we optimizing?' and 'This is a Statistical Estimation Problem, NOT a coding problem.' The conceptual flow places Probability Model and Estimator selection before Code Implementation. MMSE minimizes squared error, ML maximizes data likelihood, MAP incorporates prior knowledge. The math defines the estimator; code only implements it.

jsonData.question: After applying bias-only correction to a wheel encoder, readings are still 5% below true values. What additional calibration step is required?
options: Re-collect more bias samples — the initial estimate was statistically insufficient for accurate correction
Switch to a median filter to remove the residual proportional error remaining after bias correction
Apply scale factor correction $X_{cal} = (X_{raw} - b) \cdot s$ to eliminate the proportional measurement error
Increase ADC resolution from 10-bit to 12-bit to improve measurement precision and remove the error
jsonData.explanation: A 5% underestimate is a proportional (scale) error — bias correction only removes the constant offset, not the multiplicative error. The full calibration formula $X_{cal} = (X_{raw} - b) \cdot s$ removes both: first the constant offset $b$, then applies the scale factor $s = \text{true} / \text{measured}$. The lecture's key rule: 'Bias alone or scale alone is usually insufficient. Use both together for high-accuracy measurements.'

jsonData.question: A mobile robot implements gyroscope auto-zeroing. Under what condition must the bias update be DISABLED, and why?
options: When the robot enters a GPS-denied environment where absolute position references are unavailable
When ambient temperature rises by more than 5°C per minute, indicating accelerating thermal drift
When the sampling rate exceeds 500 Hz, because auto-zeroing causes instability at high IMU rates
When the robot is moving — calibrating during motion treats real angular velocity as bias to remove
jsonData.explanation: Auto-zeroing must ONLY update bias when the robot is confirmed stationary (wheel speeds ≈ 0, no vibration). If the bias estimate is updated during motion, the algorithm interprets real turns as bias to correct away — the robot would ignore actual rotations, producing catastrophic orientation errors. The lecture warns: 'If you calibrate while moving, you will calibrate out the actual motion.' GPS denial (option A) is unrelated to this logic.

jsonData.question: In robotics, a map is best described as which of the following?
options: A structured environmental representation used for planning and navigation.
An exhaustive accumulation of all raw sensor readings stored for later post-processing.
A GPS-based coordinate system for tracking the robot's outdoor position accurately.
A sequential log of visual images captured by the robot's onboard cameras over time.
jsonData.explanation: A map is defined as a structured representation of the environment that a robot uses for planning and decision-making. The key word is 'structured for use' — not raw data storage. Option B describes a sensor log, which is input to mapping but is not a map itself.

jsonData.question: What does the acronym SLAM stand for in robotics?
options: Sensor Localization and Mapping
Simultaneous Localization and Mapping
Sequential Learning and Motion
Sensor-based Localization and Modeling
jsonData.explanation: SLAM stands for Simultaneous Localization and Mapping — the robot builds a map and estimates its own position at the same time. 'Simultaneous' is the critical word, distinguishing it from sequential approaches where mapping and localization are done separately.

jsonData.question: According to the log-odds interpretation in occupancy grids, which statement correctly describes a cell where L < 0?
options: The cell is very likely occupied, with probability significantly above 0.5.
The cell has not yet received any sensor observations from the robot.
The cell is likely free, with occupancy probability below 0.5.
The cell value is invalid and must be reset before further updates.
jsonData.explanation: In log-odds: L > 0 means likely occupied (p > 0.5), L < 0 means likely free (p < 0.5), and L = 0 means completely uncertain (p = 0.5). A common mistake is confusing L < 0 with 'invalid' — negative log-odds is a valid and meaningful state indicating free space.

jsonData.question: Which of the three standard map types uses labeled real-world objects as its primary representation?
options: Metric map — represents the environment using precise geometric coordinates and shapes.
Topological map — models the world as a graph of connected places and transitions.
Occupancy grid — divides the environment into cells marked as free, occupied, or unknown.
Semantic map — labels objects like doors, chairs, and road lanes in the environment.
jsonData.explanation: Semantic maps store labeled objects such as 'Door', 'Chair', or 'Road lane'. Metric maps encode geometry (coordinates, grids), and topological maps encode place connectivity as graphs. A self-driving car's HD map actually combines all three: metric GPS coordinates, topological lane graph, and semantic labels like 'stop line'.

jsonData.question: Why do occupancy grid maps store probabilities between 0 and 1 rather than simple binary occupied/free values?
options: Sensors are noisy, making absolute certainty about cell states impractical.
Binary values demand more memory than continuous probability values in dense grids.
Probability storage is more computationally efficient for 2D array data structures.
Robot processors are specifically engineered to handle floating-point range computations.
jsonData.explanation: The probabilistic approach is motivated by sensor noise — physical sensors are never 100% accurate, so assigning absolute 0 or 1 would misrepresent reality. Options B, C, D are false: binary values actually use less memory (1 bit vs 1 byte), and probability storage is not inherently cheaper computationally.

jsonData.question: The 'circular dependency problem' in robotic mapping refers to which fundamental challenge?
options: Sensor data must be collected before the robot can begin building its map representation.
Building a correct map requires known poses, and knowing poses requires a correct map.
Loop closure detection depends on data association, which itself depends on loop closure.
Memory constraints force the robot to choose between storing poses or storing map data.
jsonData.explanation: The circular dependency is: you need accurate localization to build a correct map, but you need a correct map to localize accurately. This is why pure mapping (assuming a known pose) fails in practice — odometry drifts, IMU has bias, GPS fails indoors, and errors compound in a feedback loop.

jsonData.question: Why does occupancy grid updating use odds instead of raw probabilities for cell belief representation?
options: Odds values are bounded between 0 and 1 like probabilities but are faster to compute.
Odds require substantially less memory than raw floating-point probability values in dense grids.
Odds lack an upper bound, so the certainty value never gets permanently stuck at 1.0.
The odds formulation is far simpler to implement in embedded real-time robotic systems.
jsonData.explanation: Raw probabilities saturate at 1.0 due to finite floating-point precision — once stuck at 1.0, multiplying by any Bayesian update keeps it at 1.0 forever. Odds transform the range from [0,1] to [0,∞), giving infinite headroom so beliefs remain flexible even after thousands of consistent readings.

jsonData.question: In the EKF-SLAM covariance matrix, what do the off-diagonal terms specifically encode?
options: The independent positional uncertainty of each individually observed landmark in the map.
The total count of sensor observations incorporated into each landmark's estimate.
The confidence level for each dimension of the robot's current pose estimate.
How uncertainty in the robot's pose propagates to affect landmark position estimates.
jsonData.explanation: Off-diagonal terms encode cross-correlations — specifically how robot pose uncertainty propagates to landmark estimates and how landmarks are correlated with each other. The diagonal terms store individual uncertainties (robot pose, each landmark). This cross-correlation tracking is what makes EKF-SLAM statistically consistent but also computationally expensive.

jsonData.question: Which of the following best describes the representation used by a topological map?
options: A graph structure encoding places as nodes and transitions between them as edges.
A dense 2D array of probabilistic occupancy values distributed uniformly across the mapped environment area.
A 3D point cloud reconstructed from depth sensor measurements taken over time.
A collection of semantically labeled objects positioned in a precise metric coordinate frame.
jsonData.explanation: Topological maps represent the environment as a graph — nodes are places (rooms, intersections) and edges are connections (corridors, doors). A metro map is a classic topological map. Unlike metric maps, topological maps do not store precise geometric coordinates, which makes them memory-efficient but less accurate for obstacle avoidance.

jsonData.question: In SLAM, data association uncertainty refers specifically to which of the following challenges?
options: The difficulty of predicting how accumulated sensor noise will corrupt future map updates.
Deciding whether a newly observed landmark matches one already stored in the map.
The inability to process multiple sensor streams simultaneously on limited hardware.
Maintaining a consistent global coordinate frame across multiple separate mapping sessions.
jsonData.explanation: Data association is the correspondence problem: 'Is the landmark I see now the same one I saw before?' If a hallway has ten identical white doors, picking the wrong one corrupts the entire map. A single wrong data association can cause divergence — the robot's estimated position drifts irreversibly from the truth.

jsonData.question: Why does 3D SLAM require significantly more memory than 2D SLAM for an equivalent environment size?
options: 3D sensors generate much larger raw data files that must be stored alongside the finished map.
3D SLAM algorithms require full covariance matrices whereas 2D SLAM algorithms do not need them.
Adding a third spatial dimension causes memory consumption to scale cubically rather than quadratically.
3D maps must additionally store semantic labels per voxel, consuming substantial extra storage overhead.
jsonData.explanation: In 2D, memory scales as (W/r)×(H/r) — quadratically. In 3D it becomes (W/r)×(H/r)×(D/r) — cubically. A 100×100×10m volume at 10cm resolution yields 10⁸ voxels (~100 MB for occupancy alone), and that excludes color, semantics, or uncertainty data. Options A and D describe additional costs but are not the fundamental reason.

jsonData.question: Loop closure is described as 'the most important breakthrough' for a SLAM system. What makes a successful loop closure so impactful?
options: It allows the robot to determine and verify its absolute starting position reliably without any external GPS reference signal at any point.
It enables the robot to simultaneously track multiple moving obstacles within the surrounding environment.
It reduces instantaneous sensor noise by averaging measurements over multiple map revisit events.
It corrects accumulated drift by realigning poses when the robot returns to a known location.
jsonData.explanation: Over time, small odometry and sensor errors accumulate into significant drift. When the robot recognizes a previously visited location (loop closure), the accumulated error is distributed back through the trajectory, dramatically improving global map consistency. A false positive loop closure is equally dangerous — it can cause the map to distort or collapse entirely.

jsonData.question: A grid map covers a 10m × 10m area at 5cm (0.05m) cell resolution. How many cells does it contain?
options: 40,000 cells
4,000 cells
400,000 cells
200 cells
jsonData.explanation: Using the memory formula: (width / resolution) × (height / resolution) = (10/0.05) × (10/0.05) = 200 × 200 = 40,000 cells. At 1 byte per cell this is 40 KB — very manageable. Option B forgets to apply the formula to both dimensions. Option D only computes one dimension.

jsonData.question: In the log-odds update formula L(mᵢ|z) = L(mᵢ) + L(z|mᵢ) − L₀, if the current log-odds is L = 2.2 and the new sensor reading contributes L(z|mᵢ) = −2.2 with prior L₀ = 0, what is the resulting updated value?
options: L = 4.4, reflecting strong combined certainty of occupancy from both the prior and the new reading.
L = 0, meaning the cell has returned to a completely uncertain state.
L = −2.2, meaning the new reading alone determines the cell state as likely free.
L = 2.2, because log-odds values cannot be reduced below their prior accumulated value.
jsonData.explanation: Applying the update: L = 2.2 + (−2.2) − 0 = 0. A log-odds of 0 corresponds to p = 0.5, meaning complete uncertainty. This illustrates the flexibility of log-odds: conflicting evidence from a previously-certain cell can pull it back to uncertainty immediately, unlike raw probabilities that saturate. Option D is a common misconception.

jsonData.question: An EKF-SLAM system is tracking L = 500 landmarks. What is the total dimension N of the joint state vector?
options: N = 500, representing only the landmark positions.
N = 1000, representing two coordinates per landmark.
N = 1003, from the formula N = 3 + 2L where 3 is the robot pose size.
N = 1500, because the formula N = 3 + 3L accounts for three pose dimensions per landmark across the full trajectory history.
